item.title: Icarus: Testing the Limits of What a Browser Can Do
item.description: How I pushed the browser to run my offline tools, from a QR generator to a face-tracking avatar twin, and what it taught me about edge compute, privacy and knowing when to stop.
item.content:encoded:
Hey,

It's Bee again.

Some people do not know where to stop... and when. If Daedalus had told me not to fly too low or too high, my fate would have been like Icarus's. In recent weeks I have been making a bunch of small tools. Most probably you will find a use for one or two, so please check them out.

The context

Remember Vision-SL and how the browser kept doing stuff so that the server would work less? So yeah, I went on a wave of tinkering around to see what I could do lol. If you haven't noticed, I run my blog and my tools on GitHub Pages, which is free and only serves static pages. This comes with a few problems that inspired the architectural design behind the apps:

  1. I do not have the compute to process data and stuff, which is why I push for your machine to do all the work.
  2. I cannot save data anywhere (I have options, but I do not see the need to have your data or track who uses what app).
  3. I come from an era where people made apps for fun, so no, I do not intend to monetize the apps.

The vision

I might be one of the crazy ones. However, I believe that if we distribute compute power and push some of the operations to the user, we save a lot on costs. If my app can run on 4GB of RAM and use your 8GB of RAM to serve and save compute, that means I can charge less for my services. Then again, we are now in an era where surveillance reigns supreme, and I believe that users (me included...) do not trust systems. (I wrote more about this in Data-Sovereign AI and Automated Workflows.) So what if we could make sure that no data leaves your device? (The only app that sends data is the QR Generator, which checks the availability of the entered URL.) See, I am one of you guys, and I make stuff for people like us.

So we made stuff that runs offline

Think of it: your machine sends a request to my server, which serves static files, but thanks to JavaScript, it sends code you can use to do stuff. First it was the QR generator, which would generate and download offline. (The catch is that you have to wait for all the tools to be received from my server first, but after that you can cut off the internet and use them forever... or for the few days I actually used to test.) Then there was the business card maker, and then the flyer generator. The browser would save the structure and instructions, then allow you to customise. Just like that.

.... then came evil thoughts

In every sport, the history makers are those who dared to test the limits. Be it Ronaldo shooting from 40 yards out, Bolt thinking what if someone did sub-9 seconds in the 100m?, or so many incidents like that. And I wanted to join the club. So I asked myself, what if I could test / taste the limits of what the browser could do for me?

  • The first idea was a rock-paper-scissors game that ran offline, and you would actually play with your camera on. Well, that would have been fun, but then it was the same use of hand-tracking, and I am kinda tired of tracking hands lol (I already did that in No Data, No Problem). So as I was asking myself what else I could track, an idea came. Gestures. Facial expressions. And then what? That brought me to the next stage: tracking and giving feedback was light work. I wanted the browser to work. So I settled on making an avatar twin that captured expressions, translated them to the avatar and saved a video of the avatar. All offline.

Setting to work

And so I did that. Just like that. Track the eyes and mouth, and make the avatar do monkey see, monkey do. Easy peasy, right? I mean, I could just prompt it to life.... The funny thing is that when I tried, it worked. But if there is one thing you should know by now, it's that we do not just want it to work; we want it to work the right way. Initially:

  1. There was heavy lagging as the browser used resources to track images, draw outlines and make stuff move.
  2. The models being transferred to the browser were 37 MB. For a Zimbabwean user, that is way too much to transfer without even using the app.
  3. On my 16 GB RAM machine, it worked fine. On my phone, it was a bad UI.

.... back to the drawing board again

To make it usable for me and the few who will ever visit my stuff, I set out to design a better experience. As I did so, there were a few lessons that I got to learn, and trust me, it was kinda fun.

  1. Less is more. Reduce the resolution to 480p: smaller sizes (17MB) and less lagging. Reduce the model artefacts and weights being downloaded: less wait (pun intended). Reduce clutter: less control but more oomph in the design. By the time I was done, the avatar could mimic in near real time, and it now worked on my phone.
  2. Data privacy still remained. The idea never changed. The approach did. Sending data to a server for processing was an option that was intentionally never exploited. The browser ended up doing the work.

As I built the next app, another thing happened. A eureka moment. A real use case (this was just inspired by testing the limits of browser computing). The teleprompter app. The core concept never changed, just the implementation. What's even more amazing is that the app could cache relevant files in a Progressive Web App kinda way. I have a downloaded shortcut on my phone that I use now.

Up next, I have had this idea of turning these blogs into a podcast. Will I use the teleprompter? Or the avatar? Time will tell, but one thing is clear to me now. Edge compute has a limit, and as I think about my next app, I will try to be kind to your browser.

Sincerely

Yours Truly

item.title: Data-Sovereign AI and Automated Workflows: Building Fung.ai
item.description: Data-sovereign AI without handing your data to someone else's computer: how I built Fung.ai, a private AI worker on open-weight, tool-calling LLMs.
item.content:encoded:
Hey,

I'm Bee.

When your worker starts snooping on your personal mail and sharing your details, you don't stop the work that they do, nor do you keep acting as if nothing happened. You look for another worker, one that you can trust to do the job well without sharing your sensitive data. These maids, butlers, henchmen or whatever title they hold become key to your operations and over time you rely more and more on them.

Sovereignty as an infrastructure problem

In the age of AI, a lot of data is shared as people try to integrate AI (Key word - try) within their day to day work. In minutes, tasks that took hours will be done and dusted. As we try to make sure that work is done faster and better, we add more information to the AIs that we use. For context. For reference. And for experimentation. Where does this information go? Who has access to it? And what do they eventually do with it?

Without being paranoid, these questions are asked when you deal with sensitive data, with secrets, strategies and personal data on a day to day basis. With legislation that exists, your customers even ask you what you do with their data and you have to get consent to do certain things with their data. Blah, Blah, Blah. In other words, you need control over what happens to the data and where it goes. For government, the health industry and many other industries, this means that somehow you limit how AI is used. And in big 2026, saying no AI instead of more AI is shooting yourself in the foot. Firstly, your own team will still use AI whenever they can (The AI craze has swept wider and faster than Bieber fever ever did), and you risk being labeled backwards and anti-progress.

..... so how do we get AI without losing control?

We want to protect data. Data is shared via the internet. And stored on the internet. Then processed on the internet. Then the internet is mainly cloud something - cloud computing, cloud storage, etc. And cloud is someone else's computer (popular programmer joke). Whoever owns the computer or can access the data as it is transported invades our privacy, secrecy or our contract to preserve the clients' confidentiality. The problem was also highlighted by Paul Everitt at PyCon ZA (interestingly, I have also been pointing this out since 2024). AI over the internet exposes data and anyone responsible for the data is at the mercy of consequence. Another thing that also happens is jurisdiction over data issues. If the data is out of Zimbabwe, there is little that Zimbabwean courts can do to protect your data. And for an individual like me, that's scary.

.... breaking down the chain

So two surfaces that expose the data - AI and the internet. For each, we can do something. With the internet, we can host our apps and services locally. Some institutions do. The data, networks and gateways to the internet are something that we control. With providers like Google and AWS, you can even set Virtual Private Networks. However, this is only part of the equation. What use would it be to do all that and still surrender the data willingly because we want to use AI? Which is where the second part comes in, using open-weight models that power different AIs out there. Instead of using Google AIs, you can use their model Gemma - which is built from the same research as Gemini. Pretty cool, right? And that was the direction we were taking with Fung.ai.

....enter Fung.ai

Fungai means think. Something that I was trying to create. An artificial brain that is able to execute tasks without relying on external AI providers. The idea behind it was that:

  1. It should be hosted on a private network/ server (blackboxed)
  2. It should execute tasks that let business operate autonomously and efficiently
  3. It should be easily integrable with any system.

This is one digital worker whom you could put within your system and it would give you AI services without sharing your data. It worked on my PC, with a dynamic Data Analyst persona (skills + tools) that could take any dataset no matter how large, look at it, clean it and then visualise and interpret the data. I even tried it with a 40MB CSV; my machine froze a bit, but it worked.

...ripping apart the brain

With an LLM, we had something that could get text and give related text back as output. A parrot, as others would say. However, looking at recent LLMs, they are past parrot territory. More of monkey see, monkey do. Realising this, I knew that I could give it exhaustive instructions and it would try to produce text that followed suit. It kinda worked.

...... until I realised that for so many ops, I had to create very large prompts and then feed in step by step procedures to be followed. And that was too much, especially if I wanted to create so many automated operations. That is when I looked for a specific kind of model - tool-calling Large Language Models. My street explanation is that these are models that can get a list of instructions (tools or functions) and given some input they would choose the right one(s) for the context. This allowed me to now create a tool for each individual operation I wanted and even chain some and at the end of the day, the model that I chose did great (Thanks Qwen2.5).

With so many tools, I now had to define which role uses which tools and at the end of the day, as someone who wanted to automate so many business functions, I ended up creating skills - which bore instructions on what tools could be used and the tone and context for replies given for different ops. Which created a new thing for me. A persona. The skill(s) + relevant tools. This allowed me to execute a couple of operations autonomously. Given the fact that this was all done on a personal PC and without live data, I am cautious about claiming that this is a groundbreaking revelation.

I still seek opportunities to test this out to see the eventual performance in real life and real time settings. But what I am proud of is the fact that for a proof of concept, it works.

.... so what does it mean?

For me, this closed a concept I have always thought of. Owning the means of transferring data, blackboxing access to it and integrating AI meaningfully. Under demo settings, it works. And as a proof-of-concept I aim to close off the POC and maybe resurrect it in the future for research or improvement as a hobby thingie.

So this kinda wraps up my technical session on my blog and proceeding from this, I will be writing about anything and everything. Can't wait to see you next time.

Sincerely,

Yours truly

item.title: Designing Vision-SL: A preview into what we considered
item.description: One might call it undiagnosed ADHD - the way I get stuck on a problem, break it apart and try to find a solution. Vision-SL is one project that brings that to light, and today I am gonna break apart what made it interesting to me.
item.content:encoded:
Hey,

I'm Bee.

One might call it undiagnosed ADHD - the way I get stuck on a problem, break it apart and try to find a solution. Vision-SL is one project that brings that to light, and today I am gonna break apart what made it interesting to me. I hope you remember that in No Data, No Problem, I touched on the context of the problem. No Zimbabwe Sign Language data exists and, well, I wanted to create something that fills that gap. What's crazy about it all is that it started with simple questions and became complex product design over time.

Flirting with languages

Hello. Bonjour. Mhoro. Salibonani. Similar meanings but different languages, different compositions and constructs. In the four words above, there is no way that the contexts, compositions and constructs can be translated from one language or one form to another. Mid last year, I wrote an abstract for consideration under one of the POTRAZ funding opportunities to collect data on the sixteen official languages in Zimbabwe, and another one under a Mozilla program (Shame on me for forgetting the actual name - in my defense, I am writing offline and I might check later). All I wanted was to have a starting point for local language data to train, fine-tune and create LLMs that are fluent in local languages. Whether these failed to be considered because of relevance, my capacity to carry them out or the way I wrote the proposals - I might not know. But neither ever came to life.

Back to the basics (again)

Borrowing from neuroplasticity and how children learn, I thought to myself: what if the reason why AI can never fully speak to the local context is the fact that we try to translate from one language to another? A child needs to learn from contextual content to be fluent, rather than being told about concepts in a foreign language (not verified, my AI reviewers keep flagging that I need to support this with scholars, etc.). Upon realising that no one really cares about creating the basics (Disclaimer: from my circles) - the corpus, the infrastructure, etc. - I took it upon myself to try as much as I can. One man can change the world, as Big Sean said. The first was through the Shona words scraper. And the second was Vision-SL.

One mission, two approaches

For the corpus, I needed reference material to dissect the Shona language. I needed something that I could use to study the relationship between words, their classes, etc. And I found what I was looking for - from multiple sources (still to be cleaned, though). Then came Vision-SL, where the reference data was missing. How could I solve the case of missing/scarce data? How could I build on limited data? To train a computer vision model, I would need thousands of images in different contexts and settings. A near-impossible task given my skills (I am a shortcut dev, remember...). And on the off chance that I also needed to scale this to another language, would I be able to do that with ease?

Questions, questions, questions????

As I asked myself these questions, I tapped into my business analyst role for a moment. And my questions could be generalised as below:

  1. How do we create something that uses as little data as possible to train on Zimbabwean sign language?
  2. In the event that it is to be adopted for another language, how do we make it easier to set up and use?
  3. How do we create a system that preserves the teacher-student relationship without major disruption whilst having multiple benefits?

With each question, sub-questions started spinning, and our resolution was as follows:

  • The teacher is the absolute source of truth; let them teach, set assignments and evaluate responses/results from the students
  • Have a system that allows the teacher to specify whatever they are teaching, and the system would pass the knowledge to the student accordingly
  • Have a system that offers convenience to both the student and the teacher whilst minimising the teacher's effort and maximising the student's practice

.... and we did that (kind of...)

As a BA, I should have researched more; unfortunately, I didn't until the prototype was ready. Hand-tracking features were working and we could capture the images... I mean, we only needed a few thousand. With each save, the storage on the local machine was being tested (personal PC, remember) and the model could not accurately detect shapes for hand signals.

... and then came a question

What if we could use less space and store more? Another interesting thing we overlooked was how the system would work in production. So much image data was being stored and needed to be transferred, processed and trained on at times. For the Zimbabwean context, that was a non-starter - our system was simply conceptual. Hopefully, with time, others would improve on it.

Then came the Eureka moment. Walking to work and a bit late, I asked myself why we could not save just the hand shapes and eliminate the 60% of the data used for background, etc. So I searched for how we could auto-crop and save before sending to the backend. As I was looking into this, I also came across MediaPipe and WebAssembly. What fascinated me was the fact that both of these even solved problems I never thought I had.

From hand images to co-ordinates

Learning about how a lightweight MediaPipe model could read a hand and use 21 co-ordinates in the x, y, z axes was a game changer. I began thinking about how I could convert each hand image into those numbers. And then we tinkered a bit and discovered that with 3 saved sets of co-ordinates, the system could now pick up the signed letter from the student side (after adding three or more different letters or words). Only a negligible portion of the original payload was now being sent, so for UX, these were bonus points. Upon further research, I discovered that the model could be cached in the browser and continue working, even without the internet. Further bonus points lol.

Then we discovered that we could even make the browser do the work

Whilst learning about MediaPipe, we also learned about Edge-AI, where you have AI services doing the work at the point of interface between the user and the system (better definitions exist online). Within the browser, we could have MediaPipe doing the hand recognition and co-ordinate extraction, and then the model would be trained on/refer to the co-ordinates. This came with so many advantages:

  1. User privacy - we don't store user pictures, etc.
  2. Reduced payloads - better user experience, especially in Zimbabwe where data costs a lot
  3. Reduced server specs for eventual deployment

Then it even went a step further

As this eventually came to life, another concern came up. Offline access. For the students who really need the solutions. And we ended up designing and developing a desktop application that had offline capabilities (before my PC crashed - we are almost done again, though).

As I take the stage at DevFest Lusaka, I will not be talking about the technical layers behind Vision-SL. There are others who can speak to that better. But I will be talking about how an open-source solution, coupled with reframing a problem and research, ended up helping me to create inclusive technology and possibly helping create the backbone of sign language assistants and translators around the world. Maybe in a future article, I will dive into the limits of what I did and where I feel I still need some clarity and input to make Vision-SL better.

item.title: Developer Community Events: PyCon ZA & DevFest Harare
item.description: What I learned about organising developer community events from PyCon ZA to DevFest Harare: volunteer coordination, expectations, and building for local needs.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

Funny thing: several AIs have pinpointed my monotonous intro as a weakness in my writing (I kinda use AI to review my work now and ask it how I can be better). And boy oh boy, I am not gonna change that. It has been three weeks since my last article, and I was supposed to follow up the No Data, No Problem with a technical article... up to now, I haven't.

In the past two weeks, I have travelled to Cape Town for PyCon ZA, where I gave a talk around the 16,000 jobs trilogy. Then I was organising Zimbabwe's biggest tech conference (DevFest Harare). In between the travel, talks and organising, my time to blog got limited. So let's dive into the past two weeks, and then I will share the gist of what has been up. First up: PyCon ZA.

PyCon ZA

I submitted a talk proposal and a travel grant so long ago that I had forgotten all about it. I mean, I submit talks everywhere, and the rate of rejection is so high that I fail to keep track. PyCon Kenya and PyCon Africa had rejected my submissions (when I applied for PyCons, I hazily daydreamed of a three-week multi-country PyCon tour, lol). With two rejections, I was expecting that this was another rejection.

... then the acceptance came.

Just a week before, I got an email that my talk and sponsorship request were under consideration, and they wanted to confirm if I would be able to make it. It took 37 minutes to make up my mind... 37 minutes only. Let me break this down: if you follow the news, you know that South Africa is not the place to be for foreigners (or so I thought; the entire journey proved otherwise, though). Then there was the travel logistics: it was too late to arrange for a flight, and that meant a 41-hour journey via bus (I would not recommend this unless one has to). And then there was the issue of having my leave approved, lol (thanks to my bosses for being kind enough to release me).

... and the event

Arriving on Tuesday, I only had a few hours to rest before volunteering on beginners' day for a Humble Data workshop. One of the most pleasant surprises was meeting a fellow Zimbabwean community builder, who also happened to be a volunteer for the event, and over the next few days, we exchanged ideas, advice and memorable moments. As I delivered my talk on the final day of the event, the friends garnered during the event were in full support, and for some reason, my talk (title: Agents think, let's make them act: Integrating open-weight LLM into a system for autonomous deterministic operation) had garnered some interest (including Paul Everitt, the Paul Everitt), as open-weight large language models are becoming the next trend (frontier is a big word) within the AI space. The big thing that happened is that a picture of me giving my talk was actually included in Paul's slides (yaay). Beyond the talks, I chaired two sessions, introduced multiple speakers and learnt a lot from a conceptual and technical level. When I left Cape Town, my head was buzzing (from a few drinks the previous nights) and my legs hurting from clubbing with newly found friends.

... then came DevFest Harare

Coming from Cape Town and learning a couple of things, I really hoped we could implement them in Harare for our DevFest event. The plan was ambitious: getting a thousand techies under one roof for a day packed full of talks and workshops. The speakers were there; I mean, we had five Google Developer Experts as speakers and local speakers, and we had some money to support the event. The event came to pass, and yeah, it was okayish: turnout was not close to what I hoped for; the event did not go as smoothly as I expected (hard lessons from organising; this shege is delivered to me every year in different formats, lol). The team put in a lot of effort, but a lot also fell through the cracks.

... we had pre-event workshop sessions

Special thanks to Uncommon.org, we had a Flutter workshop for absolute beginners in the morning, led by a Google Developer Expert, and another session on Rapid Application Deployment and Context Engineering & MCPs, led by another Google Developer Expert and a brilliant upcoming techie in the Zimbabwean landscape. The numbers were a third of the expected.

... then the event

Half of the expected attendance. Sessions were on point (mostly), both in terms of content and delivery. But the ooooomph was not there, a certain spark that I was looking for. Maybe it was being overly ambitious, but my expectation was that this event would be the turning point that led to our community being marketable and giving it the momentum to be the voice of indie developers. Unfortunately, the wait continues, and I take my equal share of the blame. For the majority, the event went well, but looking from the lens of what could be, I hope we do better the next time.

Back to the story and the articles

So hey, this is what has been up, and ooh, by the way, I showed my trilogy to the audience at PyCon ZA (and I was kinda proud of that, lol). So I will wrap up my article on the Vision-SL project (which will be my talk at DevFest Lusaka later on during the year). It feels nice to be back, and till next time, ciao.

item.title: No Data, No Problem
item.description: Zimbabwe's tech scene has blamed missing data for years. Here's how I stopped complaining and built with less: browser hand tracking and a Shona word corpus.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

Since my first days in the tech space (circa 2020–2021), there has been one discourse that industry and academia have always agreed on: the lack of available data in Zimbabwe. Pre-AI hype, when data science was the in-thing, I was one of the people who echoed that.

Fingers were always pointed at governments and institutions for not sharing their data. The hypothetical benefits of sharing data made up half the talks at every event I was part of... And it was true. As a young developer advocate, it made sense to me. We wanted the data to innovate. To drive impact. And we wanted it then.

Fast forward to 2026

Guess what??? Same echoes. Louder. The voices might have changed, but the message is still the same. Then I sit down and ask myself the question: what have we done in the past five years as tech community leads and tech communities? In the words of Joyner Lucas, "If I am not part of the solution, then I am part of the problem." My sentiments exactly. Not to be generalised across the tech ecosystem — this is what I feel about myself.

Then a belief came...

Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country. — John F. Kennedy. Great words to live by, and to be honest, ever since I heard them in Barack Obama's documentary, Yes, We Can, I have subconsciously lived by them. I suspect that is what powers me to do everything I do. I reflect on what's going on and think to myself, What small things can I do to change the outcome, to have an impact... even a minimal one? Now, back to the data story: every time I echoed that sentiment, I became more ashamed of whining rather than doing something.

...and some small things followed

The first thing that came was this: build what you can with what you have, and create leeway for others to improve or add on to what already exists. Hence the jobs scraper. Or create the data backbone and foundation from scratch and let it just sit around. Hence a large dataset of scraped Shona words. All bound to be openly shared and possibly open for collaboration (if anyone ever takes an interest in this).

First things first, use what you have

If I were to pose the question to the rest of the dev community: is the available data so utterly unusable that all we can do is complain? Then what can we do about it, besides lobbying for five years with no tangible results? In one of the things I have worked on — a sign language teaching assistant — that is exactly what we were faced with. Not much data on Zimbabwe Sign Language to train a model on. And zero idea of what Zimbabwe Sign Language looks like.

So with a mentee (full disclosure here: it's not my project), we set out to figure out what we could do to make sure we created something that used as little data as possible. Then we thought, how about we track hands and save them, so that once a student signs a letter, we can reference the closest match? That was the initial plan — but something changed. Like Archimedes getting his Eureka moment in the bath, my solution came as I was walking to work, bumping Kendrick Lamar and pondering the challenge. Hand tracking has been practised for years — a very cool party trick at data science festivals and tech events. So something must be available for a shortcut developer like me to use.

And there was — MediaPipe. It could track hands as 21 coordinate vectors. As the icing on the cake, it could do that ALL WITHIN THE BROWSER. Never had I had a better Eureka moment. Like, man, it even solved problems I never knew I had. Like privacy. Like a reduced payload size to lower end-user costs. Like low latency. The browser would simply convert images into coordinates. I will go deeper on this in another article, so for now let's get back to the topic (sorry, my mind tends to drift a bit).

As I tried to understand the mechanics of MediaPipe, a new concept was presented to me — representation learning. In this case, a complex input such as an image is abstracted down to only the meaningful information needed. Where I had thousands of pixels of layered information, including background and subject, only 21 coordinates would be taken and used. Whilst technical, it also reminded me of another approach we could use to solve some of the problems we encounter: reframing the problem to arrive at a solution with fewer resources. The result was actually interesting — with 3 sets of coordinates, the assistant could confidently map out a saved sign, and with as few as five signs, we could train a model on vectors that offered feedback when evaluating signs.

Secondly, back to the basics

Systems need data. Repeat after me — systems need data. And if it does not exist, then try to help source it. Since 2024, I have been fascinated by the fact that a fluent speaker needs at least a thousand words in a language. With access to the open internet, why then are LLMs bad at Shona? Then an assumption dawned on me: we try to understand Shona through a translated lens, or some other technique I might be unaware of — be it fine-tuning, transfer learning or direct translation. So I set out to do one simple thing: collect my one thousand words. (Release the scrapers — honestly, it's concerning that 40% of what I do in my free time is scraping.)

Working with my scrapers, we went through multiple sources where Shona translations are found (mostly religious sources and Wikipedia). In this project, the dataset is the artefact. The final product. Just words — sitting. Waiting for something to happen. Maybe this is poor man's infrastructure I am focusing on, but I just wanted the words sitting there. Waiting for something to happen.

As I gathered the words, something interesting happened. A huge portion of the words from the sources I used (~25%) were non-Shona (numbers or other languages). Which brought me to an interesting task — how to weed out the non-Shona words. Which led to the next step: actually cleaning this massive dump of words (corpus is the word to use).

I had some help

I know, this sounds like a Post Malone feature, with Morgan Wallen I guess. But to some extent, I would like to acknowledge that in the work I have been doing, I have had some people chipping in. With Vision-SL, our proof of concept could detect gang signs (honestly, those were the only signs we could spell, lol). With the aid of researchers, we could actually train on real signs, and some of the things we had not factored in were brought to light.

Limitations

Remember, I once said that just because it works doesn't mean it works the way it should. While my approaches seem to work at the prototype phase, I believe there is still a lot of work, research and experimentation to be done. Sign language has motion signs, facial expressions can tell more than just fingers, and the Shona language is more complex (I am still figuring some of the stuff out). Some cases of missing data still need the actual data, not representations or these makeshift shenanigans I get up to at times.

At the end of the day, no data, no problem. I will use what I have to do what I can. When all I could do was shout, I did. Maybe now it is time to try to create, by example, a culture of individual contributions towards what is lacking. Hopefully, this will transition Africa from simply complaining to proactively addressing some of the stuff that acts as our hurdles.

item.title: Scraping 16,000 Jobs: ETL vs ELT and Lessons Learnt, Finale
item.description: To wrap up the series, I will be talking less about the hands-on tech stuff and reflecting on the lessons learnt. The basics matter. ETL vs ELT.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

In the past two articles (Part 1 and Part 2), I have been going on about the thought process and the hands-on application of the concepts I ended up adopting. To wrap up the series, I will be talking less about the hands-on tech stuff and reflecting on the lessons learnt.

The basics matter

In two cases, my work would have been easier if I had known the basics. To be specific:

  1. The approach to just get data, extract the info and then tabulate it is not as simple as A, B, C
  2. If I had known the different ways of scraping data, I wouldn't have spent a few days learning Selenium and how to extract from WordPress

I have always prided myself in being self-taught. Then I coined the term 'short-cut developer' to describe myself. I am proud that with no academic or guided foundation, I got on the internet and taught myself to code. But I am also aware of my limitation that things should not just work. They should work effectively, efficiently, accurately and a bunch of other important words if a system is to serve its purpose. Back to the story.

ETL vs ELT

Extract. Transform. Load.

I had heard about the abbreviations before. I had a rough idea, but I didn't know where they applied. I guess booksmart is not really street smart. In my flow it was something like this:

  • Getting page content about a job from the internet (5 seconds)
  • Extracting the actual fields needed using an LLM on my machine (2-6 minutes and totally offline)
  • Writing to my local database (~1 second)

So initially I would get what I want after a few minutes. That worked!!! Now imagine this at scale. To cycle through 16000 jobs would take about 533 to 1600 hours of continuous compute. That is like 22 continuous days at least. The process where I obtained the page, extracted the info (transformed it) and then left it for my colleague to load it, is ETL.

The cure to my pain

Hidden from my plain sight was a principle that applies when you have such a problem. I could just store as many jobs as possible on my personal computer and then do the transformation at my own time. That is what ELT does. In my case that was the best approach because:

  1. If my internet went down - work could still go on
  2. I could provide up-to-date data to my colleague at regular intervals

To top it off, I could run a few things at the same time. To achieve that, I ended up indexing all the pages that had job listings. Then following that index, I could load page by page to my local dump for the raw job text. At times, using concepts like threading, I was able to achieve that. Then in the background the transformation would be taking place.

Another thing that came to mind is the fact that maybe in the future, if I realise that I missed something key, I could still get the raw dump and transform it again. (I did that, interestingly, I could expand on the already loaded data)

Disclaimer

One might argue that what I did is still ETL. Technically, depending on where you draw the boundaries of extraction and transformation, they could be right. But the important difference for me was what happened after I received the data.

Instead of transforming every job immediately, I extracted the raw content, loaded it locally, and transformed it later.

Extract. Load. Transform. ELT.

A bit about scraping

I think in the first article, I talked about the different approaches that I adopted as trial and error. And the key takeaway was that different strokes for different folks, I guess. Another thing that I should address is whether this was done the right way. There are a lot of grey areas when it comes to scraping content that is in the public domain. I did this under the guise of educational research and the data is not for commercial use. I also adopted respectful scraping to avoid flooding the sources with multiple requests. And I am also open to discussing methods of respectful scraping that I can adopt in the future.

Writing this series is not merely about documenting my "genius moments", but sharing the realisation that being a short-cut developer has its own limits. Building something real makes you realise the shortfalls and at times eating your shoe, admitting and acknowledging your limits is the only way to grow. And aha, I now know where to use ETL. 18,693 job posts say so :)

Finale. Curtains close.

item.title: Scraping 16,000 Jobs: Mapping Zimbabwe's Job Market, Part 2
item.description: How I used a local LLM, tool calling and Pydantic models to turn thousands of scraped Zimbabwean job posts into clean, structured data. Part 2 of the build.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

In Part 1, I left off with three questions: how do I store the data, how do I process it, and how do I make sure my colleague has something she can use? Let's pick up right there.

When things connect for the first time, it feels like pure bliss. Until you start asking yourself questions. By this stage, I had scraped close to a hundred job post pages. I had this massive dump of the pages and the code within them, and I wasn't really sure how to collect the data I needed. If I searched for keywords within the text, I could pick out the words, right? Well, yes and no. There were a few factors that made this unfeasible.

  1. Inconsistencies in data structure and format. Collecting data that's two or three years old meant there was a possibility that the structure had changed at some point. An added or removed column could make my code break or miss some info at one point or another.
  2. The same job, say teacher, could be written in different ways. Teacher, Trainer, Mentor — in some cases they were used interchangeably.

For that reason, keyword searches became a non-option, since at the expected scale the scripts would break or miss some important data along the way.

Back to the human approach

I realised that a regular human would look at the data and probably tabulate the key information. I mean, if I were to look at a job list for analysis, I would probably have columns for things like the title, the location, etc. to compare. However, it would be hard to do that over and over again, 16,000 times (18,000 at the time of writing). To do that, the key things I would need are a brain that learns what to deduce and a structure to follow as I extract the info. My skills are not exceptional enough to code such a thing, but if I were to use existing and readily available technology, LLMs would do the trick.

LLM — my system brain and how I fed it

After sitting down and thinking it through, I decided on this approach:

  1. I would extract the page code/content.
  2. Then my system brain would identify what I needed.
  3. And finally, I would put it in a table.

Easy peasy, lemon squeezy, right? Well, uhhhmmm — not really. The first part was easy to work around. I needed all the content on the job post as text. Using BeautifulSoup, that was easily done. Just one line of code and pooow, I had the entire page as text.

What is an LLM?

In simple terms, think of it as the system brain that powers AI. It is a system (model is the actual term — LLM means Large Language Model) that, after being exposed to massive amounts of data, recognises patterns and is capable of performing tasks according to the given instructions. Because of advances in AI research, a few open-weight LLMs are available for download and reuse. In my case, I would just give it a block of text, and it would identify the data I wanted and pull it out. It all worked until................. (in Ray Williams' voice, lol).

.....until what?

Until I realised that as much as it could get the information, it was not giving a consistent column name on every record. If I asked the LLM to give me a title, six out of ten times it would correctly label the column (or fieldName) as title. Then there would be jobTitle, _job_title_, _title_for_the_job_, etc. This was a problem because I wanted to standardise this data and feed it elsewhere. This prompted me to look for ways to make sure it was all standardised.

Not all LLMs are created equal

LLMs are built differently, for different purposes and for different environments. One constraint I had was my computing power. At 16GB of RAM, I had more than most, but I still had to make sure whatever I chose to solve my problem would work with what I had. I ended up choosing LLMs (system brains) with a special skill called tool calling. This meant that you could define a few tools (like small helpers that execute given tasks). You could create a lot of them, and when faced with a question, the LLM would choose the right one and make it produce the right stuff.

What was the tool I ended up using like?

All I wanted was to feed the brain a bunch of text about a job, have it extract the required fields and then present the data in a uniform format. The first part was solved. The second part was partially solved — the LLM (Qwen2.5) could pick the right tool — and to cater for the last part, I had to do two things.

I created a model (different from the model in LLM)

Phew... Brandon and models, lol. I had to create what I call a Pydantic model — an abstraction of the exact structure I wanted, with guides and constraints, so that the structure was the absolute reference for what needed to be produced. Then I created a function that would be called as a tool, to make the LLM adhere to the instructions on what was needed and then give the output as requested.

And it worked.

For the technical part, this was all the heavy lifting (thinking, in this case). As a result, I was able to read the job boards, get job listings, read them and then list them out in a table (for my colleague). For now, the technical part was done, and we were definitely heading in the right direction.

A bit philosophical

Sometimes being on the right path does not equate to arriving at your destination. Pacing, tempo and strategy come into play. Beyond the technical part, which I have articulated, there is the need to strategise the process so that a handful of extracted posts could turn into a massive structured data silo that could produce insights. This was greatly emphasised during the learning process. I got lost a couple of times, and a few things broke — not because of the code, but because of the approach. This is what the finale will touch on. (No more technical stuff, I promise.)

item.description: How I scraped thousands of Zimbabwean job listings with BeautifulSoup, Selenium and the WordPress API to track rising and dying careers. Part 1 of the build.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

In Back Again, I promised to go a bit more tech than social commentary. This is me keeping that promise.

I was talking with a friend the other day, and we were discussing the job market for Business Analysts in Zimbabwe. The conversation went something like, "Hey, it seems like the job market for BAs is actually good." "Oh, really? How good is it?" At this point, picture me with a curious, nefarious look and one brow raised, and my colleague with a calculating gaze trying to figure it out. Long story short, you can't know what you can't measure, as one of my uni lecturers once said.

The conversation evolved into how many vacancies we could get from LinkedIn and other popular sources (at this point, we didn't have any other sources), and then into alternative sources of this data. I had previously had an idea of offering career guidance services using historical data. Being vocal and loud (typical me, of course), I brought that up, and my colleague asked the next questions: how will you find the other data? and how will you offer career guidance services?

Beyond the convo

Coincidentally, I had some free time, an unanswered question and a colleague with similar interests (a pseudo-accountability partner) at that moment. In those moments, my mind sparked like the Fourth of July (or New Year's Day in my country). I had a design problem, which would later turn into an engineering problem and then, well, everyone's problem, because I spent the next few months trying to talk about this. Key to the start of the project, I wanted the following:

  1. As much historical data as possible.
  2. To identify rising (emerging) and dying professions.

This led me to look for local job boards I could find on the internet and try to get the data from there.

First step

So we isolated a few job boards we could find and looked into the LinkedIn API, but most of what we could find did not specifically answer our questions. Then there was one source we thought we could get the information from via web scraping (basically writing a script to get the code behind a webpage and then isolate the info we want). It had to be done for every single page, which meant that for every job we had to have the link and then scrape it for the info we wanted. To be honest, we just looked and thought, oh, this could be important. However, we wanted to do it for as many jobs as possible (not just BA roles), which meant that there were a lot of pages to visit and record. To be honest, that was going to be tiring, and we were bound to give up at some point. So I decided to automate the process. During the automation, some things came up that I kind of had to think around.

1. What is the structure of our starting point?

For the final project, I utilised three sources (my colleague is more of a Data Analyst, so I opted to collect the data for her), and the sources had different structures. One was a regular HTML webpage, another was WordPress and the third was built with JavaScript. Each source needed its own approach, and that was the interesting part. One allowed BeautifulSoup and another did not, so I had to resort to Selenium. The third took too long to ingest, so I had to use the WordPress API (I discovered that after a few days of retries). There are many ways to kill a cat, and this time I had to try them all to find what worked at each and every turn. (I can already foresee so many questions around this. Can I explain more in the next article? Yes? Thanks.)

2. What do I press next, and how do I press it?

In whatever I automate, the key question I ask is, If I were to do this, what would be my natural next step? In this context, if I am on a page, either my starting point or a page I am reading, what do I do to go to the next page? In some instances, something as simple as ?page=2 or ?page=3 can help you navigate, up until the last page. In other instances, it doesn't work, and I had to find the button or element to click so that I am led to the next page (sorry, I will explain later if you are not that techy). That answers the latter question. As for the earlier one, I would simply extract the list of links (URLs) that led to the actual jobs. That led me to this approach:

  1. I find my starting point (let's say www.site.com/start-here).
  2. I list and save all the links to jobs that are there (www.site.com/job-1, www.site.com/job-2, etc.).
  3. Then I visit the specific page, www.site.com/job-1, and get the HTML.

3. The next problem

After all this, there were questions that I had to deal with, and I had to make sure that I countered them so that this came to life, and I am glad it eventually did. As a preview, the questions were: how do I store the data, how do I process it, and how do I actually make sure that I have something that my colleague could use? I am sure this is getting longer than I anticipated, so let me break here.

Stay tuned for part 2.

item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

And you last heard from me 20 days ago (been a while). However, I am back again (yaaaay!!!). I have a couple of articles stuck in draft mode that I could not wrap up in the past few weeks. Mainly, time has been a factor, and then there has been the issue of a bit of writer's block.

Post Article X

Reflecting on Article X, a few things popped up in my mind. This was meant to be somewhere where I articulated my thoughts and those ca-ching moments of the light bulbs in my mind. Thinking about you, my beloved reader, I felt like I robbed you of a peek into my mind. Maybe I did, but the lights were just off. Or burnt. So you couldn't see in the dark, right?

Pledge to go a bit more tech than social commentary

Also, I realised that there was too much of oh, poor me!! and less of hey, these are my thoughts, maybe they can lead to something. If it wasn't for the impromptu hey, I am back, I would just dive into the techie stuff. But be patient, ey... the lights are back on, time has been kinder as of late, and I am in jolly good spirits.

What to expect later...

A talk inspired by a meme? Remember the tech meme about Google chowing RAM? No? Okay, I guess you are not nerdy enough. Inspired by the meme and the typical African mother mantra (If you eat here, you do the work), I came up with a concept that supports a sign language app that I am working on with a mentee. It uses Edge AI and Representation Learning (fancy ways to say that we use some of the RAM Google eats to do some work on the computer so that less data is shared). Less is more; I mean, less data means more user-friendliness and privacy. Imagine selling privacy in the surveillance era (Hell, I know they are watching, I just don't know how).

Why am I even collecting 75000 unique words?

My mom is a Shona teacher, and I spent a lot of time reading Shona in my childhood (novels, the latest editions of Kwayedza and student exam transcripts). A few things came to mind as I started thinking about how the language is constructed. Crazy concepts like neuroplasticity and biomimicry came to mind. What if we could copy from the greatest designer ever: God, Allah, Yahweh or whatever name you give to Him? So right now, I kinda have a corpus of over 80000 words that need cleaning, and part of the process includes learning the basics of the Shona language (did you know that no Shona word ends without a vowel? I dare you to give me one).

Hermesphere

Well, well, well, a child from the boulevard of broken dreams has the possibility to escape. Well, for this, I would say the biggest blocker was not technical; it was actually mental. I think part of it stems from a background that always encouraged quick fixes and painting over cracked walls. I had hotwired the entire thing around an unofficial WhatsApp client because that was the hotfix for the prototype. The MVP needs a solid foundation, which is something that I am now rebuilding.

A lil bit of love

Lol, before you judge me... what did you expect? Me to be a lonely hermit stuck in an old, isolated castle, writing on a squeaky typewriter, looking all grumpy and weary? Hell no, lol. In recent weeks, I have taken some time to spend a lil time with a special someone who you will get tired of hearing about in bits and pieces.

.... and some ambition

Now, another thing that will be taking up some of my time is applications for so many things. I feel kinda stuck, and I would like to expose myself to opportunities so that I become a better person, leader and uhmmmm... other things.

So hey, it's been a moment. How have you been? I'm back, and Article X was never really my exit.

The vision

The day I chose to write, I was driven by the desire to share more about tech, ideas and what happens around me. In equal proportions. The blog was meant to be more than just a portal into my world - it was also meant to serve as a glimpse to my mind. The thought process behind every idea. A place where street education met book-smart or somewhere along the lines.

Back to article X

When I started blogging, I never saw myself get to article X (I am the guy who started a blog post that ended up having 4 episodes). So you see why this is a big deal to me.

Article X ++

What happens next? Well, the blog is shaping to be something that I don't fully grasp yet. I am attracted to writing on tech but not as a regular thought leader. I want to say something meaningful without being the boring kind of serious. I just want the thoughts to unravel as they come. If you came expecting a blog full of practical tech concepts, tips and thoughts - I apologise for letting you down. Unapologetically so. Maybe because there is a need for at least one voice that is not focused on telling you what to do - or ten things I learnt. One voice, shaky, boldly saying, hey buddy, I might be wrong, but here is what I think.

item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

One easy way to define me is the word over-fill-whatever-you-want-here. At work, I over engineer solutions (I mean why does a simple sign-up need its own microservices and stuff), in real life I overthink and at times I overwork. When asked to do something, I overdo. Some people call it strategic, some psychotic and others have their own ways of defining this cycle (man I see what I did there).

Crazy article title right?

Well, in a random episode of Legend of the Seeker, I saw a painter who got doomed when they got stuck in a magical painting of theirs, and then a clever reference from Eminem's Bad Guy reiterated that this behavior is a doom of my own making. Of course more often than not it's beneficial, but once in a while, it's detrimental to how I fit in with others.

Introducing the third eye.

Given a situation of any kind and given an opportunity to plan or advise, my input comes as a cushion against what could possibly go wrong. Even if you give me infinity resources and Hal Jordan's ring (oh, don't tell me that you haven't watched Green Lantern - it's like Ryan Reynolds's worst movie), I would still come with a cautious plan. In some or most cases, I am right to do that. Promises break, people disappoint and processes stall. If a plan is multi-step, one thing is bound to break. If a plan has multiple actors, one of them is bound to give a Razzie-worthy performance. As for promises, well don't get me started there - especially with where I come from where you get loaded with promises (is there an invisible stat board for handshakes and that? Because I see them freely and unprovoked.)

Back to the painting bro

Now having this special gift that borders between clairvoyance and outright pessimism has its own advantages. When people's heads are up in the sky with visions that have no plans (I think pipe dreams is the word), I find myself playing an Oscar-worthy devil's advocate. And in some instances that's an asset. Before the plan is finalized, I need a back-up plan to the back-up plan. Which is not a good thing because a few people have mentioned that, and I quote 'energy-sucking, vampire behavior.' However, the pictures that have come from these negatives... Oh my gosh... and at times, my concerns were just paranoia at best.

The trap

After some time the concerns turn to trust issues, issues flagged are classified as resistance and the advice offered is termed 'unsolicited'. Being continuously in situations where the third eye has to guide me means that I can't find the right time to switch this off. There was a time I could, but now, it's that personality in the shadow waiting to devour every chance of fun I can possibly squeeze out of the situations I encounter. For some reason the world outside was set on fire, with me in the painting - stuck. Maybe it all ends when I am out of the picture. When I am 80, living on a farm. Writing poetry that no one reads, legs folded hearing the chirp of nature and a warm cup of tea by my side.

And I am not complaining about that. I embrace it. But if we ever lock horns or bump heads, just know that the third eyes seeks to be prepared. Even when the mind just says go with the flow. Why do you think I switched off the comments? Maybe one day I will spill the tea.

item.title: Black Tax
item.description: The things that are certain in life are death, taxes and another thing I don't quite remember. So today I talk about one of them. Taxes - black tax , one of the few things that holds us back as we try to push in our careers.....
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

The things that are certain in life are death, taxes and another thing I don't quite remember. So today I talk about one of them. Taxes. Actually a different kind of tax - black tax. Black tax is one of the few things that holds us back as we try to push in our careers. I used to believe that it only meant the responsibilities and financial burdens that many responsible early stage professionals are introduced to after landing decent jobs and getting opportunities. Now, looking back, I believe there is much more to what black tax is portrayed as.

Responsibilities

Let's get this one out of the way. In a way I am grateful that my closest family members have shielded me from this burden. When I landed my first job, people assumed that I would automatically assume responsibilities (assuming assumptions, lol). And they were right in some way. Over the years our families invest in our futures and it's right to return the favours. But at times, we will not be in the right space yet. In my case, I had big dreams and I still needed to invest to max my capabilities, to support and to be in the right space. Like I said, my closest relatives shielded me from that tax and that freedom allowed me to invest more in myself. The ROI is minimal for now but in the future..... There is potential for bigger payouts. However, there is another tax they could not save me from because they were not even aware of it. Institutionalisation.

Institutionalisation

I first heard of the word in a Kendrick Lamar song and at first I could not even comprehend its meaning. Then I heard it in an Aspires leaders class. And then, as I started listening to hip-hop with a mature ear - I noted the patterns. Yet somehow I couldn't figure out the correct word for it until I heard the word again. Institutionalisation, a word as deep as its length in letters.

Without pulling a dictionary to get the official meaning, here is what I think it means (probably because I write offline - switching on the internet might lead me into a TikTok or X rabbit hole). But from what I get, it is the cycle of habits and beliefs passed on to generations, guided by systems and measures that are intentionally and subconsciously put into place by groups of people. Beyond its use to point out oppression, I firmly believe it passes on some good things too. Like identity. Resilience. Shared Values. And the dark side of it where I come from is black tax.

Identity

One thing that was passed to me from the systems I grew around was that silence meant obedience. In front of elders, children never spoke or questioned. Anyone with a title was never to be questioned or advised. Their words were wisdom we were supposed to feed from. Any opinions that disputed were signs of rebellion. Now, being in a space where my voice has some kinda informal (key word informal) influence, I find myself taxed when I find myself speaking. The tax is due every time I air an opinion. If I question a big organisation (sorry Econet), or a popular belief (sorry AI thought leaders), or a person (no names, still) - it's my name and reputation that are on the line. Last time it was Elon Musk and SpaceX lol, all techies were on my back. When the price hit 205, I was cooked. However, travelling around and sharing ideas and thoughts, I discovered that some, if not most, communities that are more developed have safe spaces to question and discuss these things. As a result, the kids do not hesitate to open up and discuss these things. And more often than not, I find myself in conflict as to whether I should raise questions or opinions (especially in AI) because my identity is rooted in cultures and environments where questioning is penalised. Phew... even writing this, I know someday shege will be delivered to my doorstep for this.

Confidence

When walking, pausing and thinking about your next move is okay. When riding on a motorcycle at 200km/hr (I always dream of driving a Ninja Kawasaki), hesitation can be fatal. At the bottom of the pyramid, self esteem and questioning yourself can be tolerated, but in some rooms we get into, a split-second of second-guessing yourself means you watch an opportunity fly past. Now we are in a space where our minds are cultured to question if we deserve these opportunities we come across. Sometimes we lowball applications because we have little faith in ourselves, conditioned by the environments we grew into. Since 2021, impostor syndrome has been something I have battled with. And probably the root cause of a few timeout periods in my career. As I sit with other people from other backgrounds, I realised some people had environments that boosted their confidence. My environment continuously taxes it. As much as I am almost used to that - it's a pity that it was a tax I had to pay to be where I am.

As I wrap this up (probably because I don't wanna bore you to death with a long article), I would like to highlight that this article is not venting lol. It's a result of a realisation that the black tax that we pay limits the heights that we get to reach. And sometimes the first step to fighting your demons is to recognise them. I am at a tie with mine but maybe, when you realise yours - you can conquer them. Go ahead, chump. You demon-slayer.

item.title: WTF is Econet doing?
item.description: Zimbabwe's biggest tech company is brokering AI tokens for airtime and pennies on its latest platform? Makes me wonder what business development is up to.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon, and I swear I have no beef with Econet.

Zimbabwe's biggest tech company is what? On their latest platform here, brokering AI tokens for airtime and pennies? What? Absolutely fantastic. Makes me wonder what the business development division is up to. I have to put a disclaimer. In the AI space, we can't call it a race when no one else is competing. So let's just call it space. I do not really hate on Econet ffs, hell naw. You see, their size and history are quite interesting, yet their approach is even more interesting.

Misunderstood Concepts at play.

Before you scream that Econet is focusing on bridging access to the underserved communities, please stop. Please. Who exactly is the underserved? And how are they accessing it? Via their phones and machines? Oh, paying using what? Airtime or money? Interesting. Really interesting. Anyway, Brandon, stop picking on Econet. How can I, when they make themselves an easy target? I am not really a sucker for low hanging fruit, but this time I will bite.

As much as we talk about bundling this, introducing affordable bundles for those who can't pay much for access to AI services, the concept still doesn't make sense. I have travelled to places where infrastructure lacks and the people do not have an idea of how to access the internet. If we are genuinely talking about bringing AI to the people, we would appreciate expanding the coverage to those areas. If we are talking about affordability, don't all major AI companies offer free daily trials? And by the way, kudos on the Gemini program.

Considering their scale, and the existence of open-weight models - with tooling and stuff. To those who are not technical: this is where you have a free AI that you can link to different stuff so that it can do stuff like search the internet for answers and stuff. Now, the problem with that is that it takes a lot of computing power to host, but once done, you have an AI you can run for free. Then the cost of access can be subsidised among many users to create an AI that is nearly free. That is what I would have expected when I heard about Eco AI tokens. But no. Airtime for AI. Ecocash for AI. Anyone??

Infrastructure inga wani?

Then the other issue that I got is this. Econet has a distribution network that surpasses any company in Zimbabwe. I mean, in places where no bread truck or no bank exists, I have come across Ecocash agents. Their network reach is unmatchable (I hate to admit that). I once wrote a similar thing about Meta. Distribution network. Consumer base and reach. Key differentiators that keep the two companies in play in the AI revolution. Meta is doing something meaningful. Econet? Airtime for AI. Ecocash for AI. Anyone??

Maybe I am delusional. But remember when Econet made specialised bundles for different social media applications? Unlimited access, and for given periods. Imagine something similar, but for AI apps. I mean maybe the major ones for consumers. Think about it. Would someone pay to access Gemini or ChatGPT for a week? Or a day? If I were a student - Zimbabwe's population is dominantly youth - I would pay so that I get help with my studies. And then the therapy that comes with chatbots as companions (Oh, just admit it, at one time you also used a chatbot as a confidant). Specialised bundles for this would sell faster than hot pancakes. For students. For mundane daily tasks. Etc. But then nope. Let's buy tokens to apps that offer them for free.

Pressure to perform

On paper these initiatives make sense. At least there is motion. Not movement. Motion. An acknowledgement that something has to happen. The ability to recognise an available moat. But, if we are going to be honest, the lack of imagination, not innovation, leaves a lot to be desired. I mean, the word innovation is thrown around so much that it has grossly inflated. I always laughed at Meta's efforts. Giggled at Google's products (I was there when all they had was Bard and maaan it was baaaad). But this is a new low. Every few months, a few AI produced interfaces with an idea that, even if you put it to AI, it might question the line of thinking.

As I wrap this up. Given the talent, the size and the reputation of Econet, there is a lot that they could possibly do to position themselves as a regional AI giant. As either a contributor or a distributor. Right now they are not showing a fraction of that. And considering that they are the pinnacle of innovation since the early 2000s, the tech scene might be doomed. I know it's not my place, but it is my hope that they help set the standard - as they have previously done.

item.title: Alignment: Connecting the dots like Steve said.
item.description: So uhmm, Steve Jobs was right. The man who gave the world the iPhone was correct about so many things. But one gem doesn't get talked about...
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

So uhmm, Steve Jobs was right. The man who gave the world the iPhone (I haven't received my copy yet though) was correct about so many things. But one gem doesn't get talked about enough. His commencement speech at Stanford has one thing that stuck to me - and inspired today's writing. The dots always connect when you look at things backward even though they seem too messy.

So here is my story. I was in an intro call with a few mentees from Uncommon.org. As I was presenting on optimism and a proactive approach to building the future you desire something just hit the back of my mind. A small voice saying "Wait, you yourself would not believe this stuff". And that's your gotcha there. But trust me - you will want to stick around for this. I also had a problem with motivational speakers and that's why I avoid sounding like one.

Delusions

Back to the article. Alignment. Things coming into place. Working out. Expectedly or unexpectedly. Looking at everything from now onwards feels like every action was a piece of the puzzle. When I look at it all, part of the journey was being delusional. That crazy idea that we could be more than what the crowd saw. I also believe that years of listening to braggadocious hip hop and the song High Hopes by Panic! At The Disco helped. One day, I accepted my fate to be another John Doe, the next I felt like I could be Superman. I haven't gotten my powers to fly past the atmosphere though, but I have managed to crash past the ceiling though. It is those crazy delusions that made a kid with no public speaking experience step up for TEDx Borrowdale in 2023, that crazy delusion that made me accept the opportunity to give my first international talk even though I was ill-prepared and severely underfunded. And crazy thing about it all, those delusions started forming into shape and shaping into something even more beautiful than I could fathom.

Decisions

Beyond the delusion, the other thing that helped everything take shape was the decisions made. Tough calls at times. Crazy choices more than once.

When my self esteem was shaking, I chose to volunteer and cheat. Not the exam room kind of cheating. The cheat code kind. I compromised my status to humble myself so that I could learn more, and volunteering walked me into rooms my CV could never open. On paper, none of those calls made sense. Risks with no clear benefitting steps. No pay. No title. No guarantee that any of it would amount to anything. But each one felt like a small step to improve myself, so I took it.

More often than not, I made bad ones. I own up to them. Every single one. But not a single bad call left me empty-handed, because each one came back as a lesson.

Destiny

Now, destiny. Funny word, that one. For most people it is a hiding place. A polite way of saying the cards were dealt, the script was written and there is nothing to be done about it. Destiny becomes the excuse for not changing a single thing. If it is already written, why bother, right?

I don't buy it. Not even a little. I am the master of my fate, captain of my soul and all that. Destiny is not a script you are handed, it is one you write. Mine is in my hands, and nobody else is holding the pen.

Destiny is not a script you are handed. It is one you write.

And since it is mine to write, let me tell you exactly what I am making of it. Brandon T. Unforgettable. Boyish charm. Daring.

As I wrap this up, I hope you get to understand that the direction was intentional though the breakthroughs were coincidental. A moving man meets his luck, eh? I am living testament to that. They say life meets you at your level of preparedness, it met me in motion. Barely prepared but ready to ride on the wave. Into the unknown. At my worst. With only a dream, some delusion and a few decisions to be made.

item.title: Ego or instinct?
item.description: One of the most common misconceptions about me is that I have a big ego, a lot of pride and also a bit hot-headed. To be honest...
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

One of the most common misconceptions about me is that I have a big ego, a lot of pride and also a bit hot-headed. To be honest, all those that have the privilege of saying that should probably know something:

You are what you eat and years of drinking from poisoned chalices gave me that bit of attitude.

The beginning

All we were, were just kids with big dreams, raw talent, and we knocked on several doors hoping to be guided. When we knocked, we were hopeful that the responsible people we looked up to would lend a hand. The problem wasn't the number of no's we received. It was the false yeses, the false starts and the fake promises. The outright no made us up our game, especially when there was feedback. What I am talking about is the yes men (gender neutral, btw) who would tell us that we were on the right track just to keep us away from the right avenues and tables.

What went wrong

(This part should not be mistaken for anger, but just facts) Now imagine, we get to these rooms that were previously closed to us, the long way (where people could have shown us the way...). And I am not being entitled... These were people that were responsible for shaping the trajectory of our careers. I am talking about lecturers, role models and so many offices out there. Now we get to these tables and realise that during the entire time they were gatekeeping.

And what caused the attitude

Well, when we joined the supposedly big rooms where we were not supposed to be in, there was a chance to be ushered in and be welcomed. And to be honest, I am not sure if that would entirely change our perceptions of them. Maybe they would, maybe they wouldn't. But the fact that we were looked down upon and every achievement was belittled. Where people who did not know us welcomed us, those who knew us reminded us of who we were in order to maintain their superiority. Not where we had come from. Not the journey. But the image of the lost kids. The confused ones.

Sometimes I feel like the resentment we carry is overkill. They were people protecting their position. But the next time we sit at the table and they claim that we are rude — the question will always be this. Is it ego? Or instinct. Or a reaction.

item.title: Volunteering Again
item.description: One of the few things that has always been consistent about me is the willingness to help wherever I can. With what I have, no matter how little I have to offer. No matter how irrelevant my efforts seem...
item.content:encoded:
Hi, I'm Brandon.

This follows my other article here.

One of the few things that have always been consistent about me is the willingness to help wherever I can. With what I have, no matter how little I have to offer. No matter how irrelevant my efforts seem. That belief that the compounding efforts of people like me and you are what gradually create a better environment. And from each and every contribution there is something to gain. Purpose. Perspective. Pals. Almost every single time.

What Volunteering Looks Like

From volunteering for a few things in the past five years, a few things have become clear. One of the most common misconceptions has always been that being a volunteer is doing the world a favour. It is far from that. Or at least to me. It's servitude, commitment and owning organisational/program outcomes. One of my volunteer experiences that tested that in me was my volunteer experience with Women TechMakers Onitsha. Out of school, broke and with confidence at its lowest, I stepped up to the call for online volunteers as a Python mentor. My expertise was still at junior level, but I knew the little knowledge I had was enough to help someone get started on their path.

The Challenges

With volunteering, there are a lot of hits that you will take and the biggest of them all is disappointment. I believe one of the key things that differentiate good volunteers and bad ones is how you handle disappointment. Where I expected a class, there were only a handful of learners and another tutor who was more experienced than I was. Regardless of that, I took my classes, at times on borrowed wifi, at times to one or two learners. For eight weeks. The goal never changed, the effort never changed, and over those eight weeks, I ended up with one wonderful mentee. At least there was that, right?

Then the Team Challenges

Making that continued commitment was a personal choice. What happens when you are part of a team? When the disappointment sets in. In the targets. The team. The mission. The progress. The crazy thing is that we all volunteer for different reasons. I personally do it for the love of the game. Then you meet ambitious people who want to use the opportunities as stepping stones to better opportunities. You meet fellows who are in it all for the shine. And others who are not yet sure of their commitment.

Disclaimer

I never claim that I am the best volunteer out there. There are so many better than me. I understand that programs have got different aims and I understand that there are KPIs to be reached and there are rules to follow. Sometimes I stray from that... rightfully so, but once in a while I am wrong. But I will always give all my commitment to given initiatives.

Why Mentor Again?

At the turn of the year, I was walking away from all volunteering. I had done my part. We grew communities. I mentored a few. Connected a few more. It was time to leave. Then... a few mentees reached out, grateful for the opportunities presented, the exposure and the eye-openers shared. Mostly from tagging a few friends to events, to posts, to programs. So while I can still afford a few hours a week — why not give a few hours?
