item.title: Aura vs Authority: My Talks approach
item.description: Aura farming. Aura gambling. Aura debt. One is an achievement. One is the difference between a great talk and a disaster. One is an unforgivable mistake and an unforgettable experience. Whenever I give a talk, I know the needle tiptoes somewhere between the three. And I have had my fair share of all three.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

Aura farming. Aura gambling. Aura debt. One is an achievement. One is the difference between a great talk and a disaster. One is an unforgivable mistake and an unforgettable experience. Whenever I give a talk, I know the needle tiptoes somewhere between the three. And I have had my fair share of all three.

Early days - Chasing Authority

Back when I started giving talks, I read a lot about the tips and tricks to wow an audience. Probably watched a few videos too. And all seemed to gravitate around one thing. Command authority over the stage and the audience. Pretty solid ideas... but a disaster in practice. Maybe it was inexperience, or maybe a bit of stage fright, but I always seemed to forget my lines, my voice would be shaky and most importantly, my slides would be blurry. A real embodiment of Eminem's Lose Yourself. God forbid, you watch my TEDx Borrowdale talk. That is aura debt on tape. My Falling Walls Lab presentation? More aura debt. I swear to God, the early talks would have driven me to aura bankruptcy.

Root Cause

When I reflect on it all, the cause of all this was the fact that I chased authority on stage, yet my mind was not so sure that I could ever attain it. Lowkey, some stages were bigger than I ever expected, some audiences more experienced and some stakes so high. The authority, I thought I would get from copywriting my talks, cramming movements and trying to pace my voice and movements? It was nowhere to be found. I never reshared my talks to the world, because lowkey, I was embarrassed. Some days I wished the world could swallow me whole.

The common factor

When I look at it from my current perspective, my biggest strength was always writing. Choosing the right words to suit the themes or to sell the ideas. On paper, format was the only thing that could stop me, but content, research and delivery were on point. Boy, I could sell water to a well and come back with a pre-order.

"Boy, I could sell water to a well and come back with a pre-order."

The realisation

It took some time, but what I got to discover was that the best thing about my writing and applications was never the words but the perspective. When you see tech from a ghetto point of view - you value cost, access and immediate benefit; in the rooms that I got into, they saw opportunity, legacy and revolution. Two sides of the same coin. When they saw head, I saw tail. And I could describe tail better than them. So together we had the full picture.

The aftermath - authenticity

So I started speaking ghetto in corporate, then I spoke student lingo in industry and academic set-up, then it was Zimbabwe to the world and so forth. Each talk was me at the core. The audience didn't matter. I spoke what I saw and felt (more often than not, it got me in trouble). And the more that I did, authority was no longer a priority. Crazy enough, the majority embraced the voice (which was shaky at times), the views (which were sometimes wrong) and the person behind. Where I thought I needed credibility, my raw honesty still managed to gain some credit. After four or five times - your confidence and your game become rooted in your identity and not your act. One bad talk - I am from the ghetto. One good talk - I represent the ghetto. A bad day in the office (on stage actually) could be forgotten, a good one would be applauded.

Aura Farming

Then one talk in particular changed it all. DevFest 2024. Harare Institute of Technology. I was scheduled for a talk and then it got cancelled because of time. Some earlier talks and sessions had eaten into our time. My laptop was already packed and I had even told my friends that there was no talk. Then as the organisers waited for snacks to come (I had taken a sabbatical from GDG that year), they wanted someone to hold down the crowd. Suddenly I had a chance. It was after Tine (who delivered an amazing talk btw) and the time was a little bit flexible.

The start of the talk

... As I stepped to the podium, a few cheers came from a few friends as I set up and then I looked at the audience and was like what the hell, let's take them on a story. At the core of the story were three things:

  1. I am just like you, nothing special about me...
  2. ...I discovered this cool thing that I am talking about...
  3. ...It's making me look amazing (look, I am giving a talk - it could have been you)

The inspiration

The delivery was a bit from Ryan Reynolds' playbook. First we were not taking things too seriously. There was some self-deprecating humour. Then there were a few disses to an imaginary friend. Now the story was as follows. A year ago, a friend bragged to me about computer vision, etc. This year, I discovered that I can feed video into an AI... and get the same result. And then there was the repeated catch phrase:

Like a good student, I copied. I edited. And I pasted.

The delivery

Over the course of the next 20 or 30 minutes, I showcased how Google's AI Studio allowed me to test an idea and generated code for me to use. All I had to do was to copy most of it, edit a few parts and paste it. And it worked. Like a charm. From that moment, my talks now had one MO. Go on stage, smile (this is important - if it looks devious, much better), act like your talk is dropping forbidden knowledge, speak like myself and put out a disclaimer that this might not be the best way to do it - but it works.

But it was never enough

From that talk, I discovered that relating to the audience actually made them pay more attention. It built that sense of trust. BUT I discovered, I had an appetite for something riskier. Increasing the stakes on how the audience perceived me. Aura gambling.

So the next talk and all my subsequent talks started coming with disclaimers. Things that could possibly ruin my credibility, yet could help build rapport. The first line I still recall saying was:

I am not a 10x developer...

and before I could be rated and judged,

... but I am a developer advocate.

And I then went on to explain that I know sufficient code to talk tech. And as the session went on - I had receipts. Proof of stuff built (demo phase though). Then it went on and on:

I am just a self-taught developer in...

I am figuring my way out in this but...

I know vibe coding is not all that but as a vibe coder...

and so it went on and on. Like I said, it built elements of relatability with the audiences (most of them). But in some cases, you could see the organisers facepalm.

Why that will never change from now on

When I wear my analyst hat, I can pinpoint a few reasons why the approach has worked. Some which have nothing to do with me.

  1. Gen-Z is a freaking problem - They won't listen to you based on your authority and achievements. They want something interesting. Stories can spark interest, curiosity hooks them in.
  2. Being relatable matters more than being right. Mistakes are not crimes. Authenticity trumps being correct.
  3. Aura farming with a few catch phrases, flexing a bit and grounding your progress to easily replicable steps allows the audience to take something away.

That coupled with shock value, real insights and a dashing mischievous smile, has connected me to my audiences. And with that, I am not establishing myself as a subject matter expert. Just a boy, who discovered a cool thing and is excited to talk about it. And sometimes, I repeat sometimes, that is what the audience wants.

item.title: Stone Soup Chef: Building Developer Communities
item.description: A personal reflection on developer community building in Zimbabwe: how participation, trust and shared effort helped me grow and why I keep giving back.
item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

In this blog post , I will be writing about the personal reasons behind my involvement in tech communities

For me, developer community building is shared work: people contribute what they can, learn together, and make room for others to grow. The stone soup story helps me explain why that matters.

When they said never meet your heroes - they had a point. The heartbreak that usually follows when you realise how flawed your idols are , is something I am still recovering from. And then I realise that I too , am one of them. And that disappoints me further.

Breaking the veil

'He is cooking.' , I have lost count of the number of times I have heard those words. On LinkedIn. In front of an audience. Or in some rooms that I never imagined I would even get in. One would think I'm Gordon Ramsay - but I am not. Far from it. I am just the embodiment of the story about stone soup.

Stone Soup story...

Here is my summarisation of the story , long ago a hungry traveller came across a village where there was hunger. All the villagers all had something different , but it wasn't adequate enough to feed their family. Let alone , the hungry villager too. Being cunning ,the villager told everyone that he was going to make stone soup (I think that is the original scam, lol). So he lit a fire , filled a pot with water and started stirring. Everyone gathered around to see the madness and after a while , the stranger was like , 'hey guys , soon my soup will be ready , can someone give me some salt?'. Out of curiosity somebody did , and maybe some spice too. And I guess they might have asked for a few things too.

Until one thing happened. Someone was like , 'Umm buddy , this looks promising - can I add my carrots too , and then we could maybe share the soup?' . Another did the same with tomatoes , another with onions and within some time the entire village was contributing something.... And the soup they made was enough to feed everyone.

The parallels

When I started my journey in tech communities , I had nothing. And all that I became - was because of the combined efforts of so many people I worked with , initiatives we jumped on and the support that we gave each other.

Over time , I got active within the different communities , giving my all and a bit more because I believed that together we would eat. Twenty ideas would always be better than one. Fifty minds would dwarf efforts of a genius. And one big family would always have a chance against whatever disadvantaged us..

So over time , I did my part. I stirred , I begged and I got a few people interested. The game gave me relevance , I gave it servitude - and for some time , it was a fair trade.

The game gave me relevance , I gave it servitude.

Time and time again , I have always reminded everyone that there is nothing special about me. I am not a 10x developer , I am not the greatest speaker there ever was. But I am always there to make sure we all eat. Orchestration. That's my role.

So if you ever meet me , don't be disappointed. And surely don't be in awe . I. Am. Just. Like. You. If not worse - simply a kid that is still stirring. Even long after everyone else has gone.

Why that matters

Well , if we were to be honest , the tech industry in Zimbabwe is not so good. Everything is fragmented. The research , the money , the talent and the community. All I simply try is to make sure that we borrow a bit from each section. And I salivate at what could be. I will always try - because I owe everything I am to this game. From my first talk , my first flight , some of the loves (and heartbreaks ) , my first job and my first mentors. The only way to repay back is to keep giving back.

So never meet your heroes if you are not ready to accept that they too , bleed. I am not the only one , lol. There is so many of us. As long as you accept that we are human , and recognise that we all gave this game something - you will realise that you too can give back something. So that the stone soup tastes better.

Signed

Yours Truly

item.content:encoded:
Hi,

I'm Brandon.

I don't know how many times I have reintroduced myself. But with growth , I often feel the need to. So some time ago , I made a decision - to pause posting on LinkedIn. This was not the first time - I did so in 2023 and 2024. This time it was different - more like a nail in the coffin. Somehow , there is a rude awakening for me : I might still have to stick around. Like LinkedIn still has domain authority, so as long as I still wanna be visible - I have to post those I am thrilled content.

The major reason behind the shift

One of the things that I have prided myself is was my authenticity. And it was more than just my voice , but openly sharing my thoughts , my flaws and my experiences. At times , even belittling my wins when they were not all that - a trend that bothers my mates at the pedestals that we are placed on. Now growing into different environments - it's becoming a problem especially when your thoughts appear frequently on the feeds of the people that to some extent have power to squash my growth . To avoid frequently antagonising people , I find myself here and the only way to get here is if you make the choice to press click 😏

Also SEO

Then there is this crazy idea - with AI , automation and stuff I believe a personal portfolio and blogs will do more good to me than LinkedIn will. This blog becomes the single point where information about Brandon T. Bande or rogue0015 is read by both human and machine. For the machines - at least I control the narrative , for the humans , you get to hear my side of the story too. I have used sessionize for my talks , medium for my thoughts and LinkedIn for my brand image. This portfolio will bring it all together in one place.

No more signups to read my thoughts

What good is writing , if no one reads what you write? Well , for someone whose thoughts attracts audiences ( whether its for good reasons or otherwise ) , the option to create an account to read does not sit well with me. But a blog , is just like putting it in plain sight (and you can also Google me and come to this directly ).

The no AI-pledge

In a sea of voices , the desire to stand out has made me do the unthinkable - resort to AI 😭 . Not saying that AI is bad , but when you have something too real to share there are a lot of trade offs to make. Keywords. Tone . Tags . Then AI asks to tighten certain expressions , optimize for impact etc. Once done , you would realise that it feels way different than the original piece.

Messing with markdown

Haha , so as a way to decompress I write these article......in markdown. Then use a script to optimise it for SEO and stuff. But those minutes , typing in content in raw markdown ... are a necessary distraction. As a crazy , imaginative person this is the modern day equivalence to burning the midnight oil connecting my brain to the quill

So.on a final note. Welcome to my little corner on the internet. In this corner , expect to see genius takes next to what a certain pal at a conference termed 'interestingly intelligent ignorance' .Let's chat , connect and share crazy ideas. Always feel free to connect via different platforms. I look forward to hearing from you.
